nameStory: The Painted Lichen Moth gets its name from the beautiful, artistic patterns on its wings that look like delicate brushstrokes of paint. The 'lichen' part of its name comes from its caterpillars' unusual diet - they munch on the crusty lichens, mosses, and algae that grow on tree bark, making them one of nature's tiny cleanup crews.
description: The Painted Lichen Moth is a small, delicate moth with intricate wing patterns that resemble miniature abstract art. With a wingspan of about 1 to 1.4 inches, it's roughly the size of a large postage stamp when its wings are spread. These moths belong to a large family that includes the dramatic underwing moths, but painted lichen moths are much more subtle in their beauty. You'll spot adults flying from late spring through summer in New England.

idTips.label: Wing patterns
idTips.description: Wings display intricate, lacy patterns in shades of gray, brown, and white that look hand-painted with fine brushstrokes - no two individuals look exactly alike

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small moth with wingspan of 1 to 1.4 inches - about the size of a large postage stamp when wings are fully spread

idTips.label: Wing texture
idTips.description: Wings have a slightly fuzzy, soft appearance rather than the glossy sheen of many larger moths - they feel delicate like tissue paper if handled

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a gentle, fluttering motion rather than strong, direct flight - often appears to drift or dance through the air

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: When at rest, holds wings horizontally like a tiny airplane rather than folded tent-like over the body

habitat: Look for Painted Lichen Moths in areas with plenty of lichen-covered trees, especially older forests, wooded parks, and tree-lined neighborhoods throughout New England. They're particularly common where oaks, maples, and other deciduous trees have crusty lichens growing on their bark. You'll find them from sea level up into the mountains, anywhere their caterpillars can find their preferred diet of lichens and mosses.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, so start watching for them around Memorial Day weekend. Look for them flying in the evening or attracted to porch lights.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time - adults are most commonly seen from June through August. This is when you're most likely to spot them flying around lichen-covered trees or coming to lights at night.
seasonality.fall: Adult flight season winds down by early September in New England. You might find caterpillars feeding on tree lichens during this time.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - they overwinter as caterpillars or pupae. This is a good time to examine tree bark for the lichens and mosses the caterpillars will feed on come spring.

funFact: Painted Lichen Moth caterpillars are basically living air quality monitors - since lichens only grow in areas with clean air, finding these moths is actually a sign that your local environment has good air quality!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with other small, gray moths, but the painted lichen moth's intricate, lacy wing patterns are much more detailed and artistic-looking than typical 'little brown moths.' Remember: if it looks like someone painted delicate lacework on tiny wings, you've likely found a painted lichen moth.
contextualKnowledge: While called a 'lichen moth,' this species is actually part of the same large family as the dramatic underwing moths - those big moths with colorful hidden hindwings. The painted lichen moth represents the more subtle, delicate side of this diverse moth family.
compareHints: The Painted Lichen Moth is the only species in its genus found in New England, making it unique among our local moths. Compared to its relatives in the underwing moth family, it's much smaller and more delicately patterned - while underwing moths are bold and dramatic with bright warning colors, the painted lichen moth is all about subtle, intricate beauty. Its closest relatives are other lichen moths in different genera, but none have quite the same hand-painted appearance.
